summary: Describes a Policy Information Base (PIB) for a device that implements the Differentiated Services architecture. Its provisioning classes let policy systems control the device's resources. It was published for use with COPS for provisioning, and its status is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a form that a network manager fills out to tell a router how to rank different kinds of traffic. The form is no longer used and is now historic.

subtitle: Policy database for QoS in Differentiated Services networks.

tldr.problem: Network operators needed a standardized way to configure QoS policies on routers that implement DiffServ, specifying how to classify, meter, and schedule different traffic flows.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Policy Information Base (PIB) with provisioning classes for DiffServ functional elements: classifiers (which identify traffic), meters (which measure traffic rates), actions (which mark traffic), droppers (which discard overload), and queues/schedulers (which order transmission).
tldr.outcome: This PIB was used with the COPS protocol for provisioning policies to network devices. It is now Historic, as policy provisioning and DiffServ architectures have evolved.

facts.label: Core elements
facts.value: Classifiers, Meters, Actions, Droppers, Queues, Schedulers

today: RFC 3317 is Historic. DiffServ architectures and policy provisioning approaches have evolved since its publication, and alternative methods for QoS configuration have become prevalent.

sections.title: Policy-Controlled Network Quality of Service
sections.content:
DiffServ (Differentiated Services) is an architecture for routers to provide Quality of Service (QoS) by treating different types of traffic differently. Rather than giving every flow equal service, a DiffServ router can prioritize important traffic, limit excess traffic, or shape traffic to meet network goals.

However, routers needed a standard way to receive configuration for these QoS policies. RFC 3317 defines a Policy Information Base (PIB): a structured set of configuration classes that can be sent to a router via the COPS protocol to specify QoS behavior for all the traffic flowing through it.
sections.plainLanguage: A router is like a post office. DiffServ says 'deliver urgent mail first, regular mail second.' This RFC is the form that tells the post office those priorities in a language it understands.

sections.title: Data Paths and Traffic Conditioning
sections.content:
The PIB models DiffServ processing as a sequence of steps applied to packets at each interface, called a data path. Packets enter through classifiers, which sort them into classes based on criteria (IP address, port, protocol). Classified traffic passes through meters, which measure whether traffic is within policy limits (e.g., a rate limit). Traffic that conforms or violates the rate limit is then given to actions (typically, marking with a DSCP value), then through droppers (which may discard overload), and finally into queues serviced by a scheduler.

The PIB describes these elements and how they are chained together, allowing diverse router implementations to be configured uniformly.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine an assembly line: first, workers sort packages by destination (classifier). Then, they check if too many packages came for one destination today (meter). Then they label each package with its priority (action). Then guards decide which packages to reject if the bins are full (dropper). Finally, the shipping supervisor orders the packages (scheduler).

sections.title: Classifiers and Traffic Identification
sections.content:
Classifiers identify groups of packets based on packet headers, such as source address, destination address, port, protocol type, or DSCP value. Each classifier element has a filter and a precedence to resolve overlaps.

A complete classifier must include an 'everything else' entry with the lowest precedence that matches any packet not matched by higher-precedence filters. This ensures every packet is classified. One or more classifiers can be chained in sequence, forming the first step of the data path.
sections.plainLanguage: Classifiers are sorters. One might say 'if it's from the finance department, put it in pile A.' Another might say 'if it's urgent mail, put it in pile B.' The 'everything else' entry makes sure no mail gets lost.

sections.title: Metering and Rate Limits
sections.content:
Meters measure the rate at which classified traffic flows and compare it to thresholds to determine if each packet conforms to the policy. The RFC defines a Token Bucket meter as a common parameterized example, specified by a rate, burst size, and measurement interval.

Meters can implement various algorithms: Simple Token Bucket (STB) allows bursts up to a limit, Average Rate Meter (ARM) measures average flow rate, and multi-rate algorithms (SRTCM, TRTCM, TSWTCM) measure against multiple thresholds. Conformant traffic may be treated differently (e.g., marked green) from nonconformant traffic (marked red).
sections.plainLanguage: A meter is like a bouncer at a club: it counts how many people arrived, checks if they're within the limit, and if too many came, marks the extras as 'over capacity.'

sections.title: Marking, Dropping, and Scheduling
sections.content:
Actions apply consequences to traffic, most commonly marking: setting the Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) field in the packet header to indicate its treatment. Other actions (multiplexing, replication) are implicit in the PIB structure.

Algorithmic Droppers discard packets based on queue depth and drop algorithm type. Examples include Tail Drop (discard new packets when queue is full), Head Drop (discard packets at queue head when full), and Random Drop or RED (drop probabilistically to signal congestion).

Queues store packets temporarily, and Schedulers determine the order in which queued packets are transmitted. Schedulers can use methods like Strict Priority (high-priority queues always served first) or Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ, distribute bandwidth by weight). Traffic shaping is modeled as a scheduler with a maximum rate limit.
sections.plainLanguage: After sorting and metering, traffic gets stamped with a priority label (marking), some gets discarded if the system is overloaded (dropping), and then the scheduler decides which packet to send next (queuing and scheduling).

sections.title: Expressing Device Capabilities
sections.content:
The PIB includes capability tables that allow a router to report what QoS features it supports and any limitations. These tables describe what classification criteria the device can match, what metering algorithms it can implement, what scheduler types it supports, and how many queues it can create.

When a Policy Decision Point (PDP) configures a router via the COPS protocol, the PDP consults these capability tables to understand what policies can be realized on that specific device, allowing intelligent policy configuration that matches device capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: When the policy server asks 'what can you do?', the router responds with a list like 'I can match DSCP, source IP, and port. I can implement Token Bucket and Random Drop. I can create up to 16 queues.' The server then sends policies that fit what the router can do.
